::: {.lead}
*Byte Bay* has three test phones, P5, P6 and P7, and three new games: a
rhythm game, an AR pet game and a walking game in the city. The producer
asks the team: "Which phone shows the problems of each game? Which phone do
we name on the store page?" The answers are on the specification sheets of
the phones, but a sheet has many lines, and some of them are advertising. In
lecture 4 you read a phone sheet; in lecture 7 you learned what each part
does. In this seminar you **analyse** a full phone sheet: you choose the
lines that matter for a game, match phones to games, and read the small
print. Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary specifications chipset refresh-rate touch-sampling-rate battery-capacity sensor benchmark sustained-performance compatibility bottleneck >}}

## 8.1 Read a phone sheet like a game developer

A full phone sheet has twelve lines or more (@fig-sheet). An advert puts the
camera and the screen size first. A game developer reads the sheet in another
order: first the lines that change how a game runs.

![The sheet of phone P6. The marked lines change how a game runs.](images/phone-sheet.png){#fig-sheet width=94%}

| Line on the sheet | What it tells about a game |
|---|---|
| Chipset (SoC) | how fast the CPU and above all the GPU are |
| RAM | how big a game can be in memory (shared with the GPU) |
| Display | the resolution and the refresh rate: how smooth the picture is |
| Touch sampling | how fast taps reach the game |
| Battery | how long the player can play |
| OS | which games can be installed at all (compatibility) |
| Storage | room for the game (look at the free space) |
| Sensors | tilt, turning, position: which controls are possible |

: The lines of a phone sheet that matter for games. {#tbl-lines}

Other lines rarely change a game: the main camera (only for AR or photo
games), the weight, the colours, the charging speed.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.1 — Reading phone P6"}
Phone P6 (@fig-sheet): chipset with 8 cores up to 2.8 GHz and a mid-range
GPU; 8 GB RAM; 120 Hz screen, touch 240 Hz; 5000 mAh; Android 14; 256 GB
(90 GB free); accelerometer, gyroscope, compass, GPS.

1. The GPU is mid-range: big 3D games run, but not at the highest settings.
2. 120 Hz and 240 Hz touch: smooth pictures and fast taps.
3. It has a gyroscope, so AR and aiming by turning are possible.
4. 5000 mAh: long sessions are possible. The 64 MP camera does not matter
   for most games.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Choosing a test phone by its advert: "200 MP camera, 6.8-inch screen". The
camera and the screen size say almost nothing about how a game runs. Look at
the chipset, the RAM, the display and the sensors.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/sheet-filter.html" poster="sims/sheet-filter.png" title="Sheet Filter: the lines that matter for a game" height="760" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The full sheet of your phone"}
Search the web for "*your phone model* specifications" and open the page of
the maker (or a big phone website).

1. Copy six lines: chipset, RAM, display (with the refresh rate), battery,
   OS and sensors.
2. Mark one line that does not matter for most games.

*Your result:* six lines of your phone's sheet and the line you marked.
:::

## 8.2 Which phone suits which game?

Every game loads the phone in its own way. A rhythm game needs fast taps,
but little memory. A big 3D world needs a strong GPU and much RAM, but its
taps can be slow. So the lines that matter depend on the game (@fig-needs).

![Different games need different lines of the sheet.](images/game-needs.png){#fig-needs width=94%}

Byte Bay compares its three test phones:

| | P5 | P6 | P7 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chipset | 8 cores, 2.2 GHz, basic GPU | 8 cores, 2.8 GHz, mid-range GPU | 8 cores, 3.3 GHz, top GPU |
| RAM | 4 GB | 8 GB | 12 GB |
| Storage (free) | 64 GB (20 GB) | 256 GB (90 GB) | 512 GB (300 GB) |
| Display, touch | 60 Hz, 120 Hz | 120 Hz, 240 Hz | 120 Hz, 480 Hz |
| Battery | 5000 mAh | 5000 mAh | 4500 mAh |
| Sensors | accelerometer, GPS; no gyroscope | accelerometer, gyroscope, compass, GPS | accelerometer, gyroscope, compass, GPS |

: The three test phones of Byte Bay. {#tbl-phones}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.2 — Three games, three phones"}
1. *Beat Lane* (rhythm game): the touch line decides. P5 checks touches at
   120 Hz and draws at 60 Hz, so its taps arrive latest. P5 shows the
   problems; P6 and P7 respond fast.
2. *Pocket Zoo AR* (AR pet game): the sensors line decides. P5 has no
   gyroscope: the game cannot run there. This is a compatibility problem
   (lecture 6), so the store does not offer the game for P5.
3. *Storm Realm* (big 3D world, needs 8 GB RAM): P5 with 4 GB is below the
   requirement; its RAM is the bottleneck.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Testing only on the best phone. P7 hides the problems that most players
will meet. A good test plan has a weak phone (P5), a typical phone (P6) and
a strong phone (P7), as in lecture 6.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The best game for your phone"}
Use the six lines of your phone from section 8.1 and @fig-needs.

1. For which kind of game is your phone best? For which is it weakest?
2. Give one line of the sheet as the reason for each answer.

*Your result:* two game types, each with its line of the sheet.
:::

## 8.3 Reading the small print: "up to", peak and sustained

The sheet of P7 says "up to 3.3 GHz" and "up to 22 hours of video". Byte Bay
tests it with a 30-minute match, and the game slows down after 10 minutes.
Is the sheet wrong? No: it shows the best case.

- **"Up to 3.3 GHz"**: the fastest core reaches this speed for a short time.
  When the SoC gets hot, it slows down (lecture 7).
- **"Up to 22 hours of video"**: watching a video needs little work. A 3D
  game draws much more current, so it runs for far fewer hours.
- **A benchmark** runs the same work on every phone and gives a score. A
  short test shows the **peak**; a test of 20 minutes or more shows the
  **sustained performance** (@fig-print).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 8.1 — Sustained performance"}
The **sustained performance** of a device is the speed it keeps during a
long session, after it has warmed up. The **peak performance** is its speed
for a short time, when it is still cool.
:::

![P7 starts much faster, but loses more speed when it is warm.](images/small-print.png){#fig-print width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.3 — A 30-minute match"}
Byte Bay runs a benchmark for 20 minutes on P6 and P7.

1. P6: 1000 at the start, 800 after 20 minutes. It keeps 80 % of its peak.
2. P7: 1400 at the start, 840 after 20 minutes. It keeps only 60 %.
3. For a long match, compare the sustained scores: 840 against 800. P7 is
   still a little faster, but not 40 % faster as the peak scores suggest.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.4 — Hours of play"}
The walking game *City Quest* uses GPS and mobile data and draws 900 mA on
every phone.

1. P7: 4500 mAh ÷ 900 mA = 5 hours.
2. P5 and P6: 5000 mAh ÷ 900 mA, a little more than 5.5 hours.
3. The "22 hours of video" of P7 does not help here: a game is not a video.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Comparing phones by their peak numbers only. A short test or an "up to"
value shows the first minute. Players play for 20 or 30 minutes: the
sustained speed and the hours of play decide what they feel.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your own battery test"}
Charge your phone above 50 %. Play a game for 10 minutes with the usual
brightness.

1. Write the battery level before and after.
2. If the level fell by 5 %, the full battery lasts 100 ÷ 5 = 20 times
   10 minutes = 200 minutes. Do the same for your result.

*Your result:* the two levels and your estimate of the play time.
:::

## Case study: test phones for Beat Lane

*Byte Bay* will release *Beat Lane*, a rhythm game: the player taps notes to
the music, and a match lasts 30 minutes. The game needs a steady 60 fps and
fast taps. The producer must choose the phone that shows the problems, and
the "recommended phone" for the store page. The three test phones are those
of @tbl-phones: P5 (60 Hz, touch 120 Hz, 4 GB), P6 (120 Hz, touch 240 Hz,
8 GB, benchmark 1000 → 800) and P7 (120 Hz, touch 480 Hz, 12 GB, benchmark
1400 → 840, 4500 mAh). The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses
these facts. In the mini-game below you answer the producer's questions for
five games.

{{< sim file="sims/phone-picker.html" poster="sims/phone-picker.png" title="Phone Picker: which phone, and which line decides?" kind="game" height="720" >}}

## Further reading

Tanenbaum and Austin, *Structured Computer Organization*, 6th ed., Chapter 1
(performance and the computer zoo). Android Developers documentation,
"Performance" and "Thermal API" (how games react to a hot device).

## Exercises

1. Name four lines of a phone sheet that change how a game runs.
2. Name two lines that do not matter for most games.
3. Which line decides for a rhythm game? Why?
4. Which line decides if an AR game can run on P5? Why?
5. A game needs 8 GB of RAM. Which of the three test phones is below this?
6. Why should a test plan not use only the best phone?
7. What does "up to 3.3 GHz" mean?
8. P6 scores 1000 at the start and 800 after 20 minutes. What are its peak
   and its sustained score?
9. A phone has 4500 mAh, and a game draws 900 mA. About how long can the
   player play? Why is "22 hours of video" no help?
10. *Beat Lane*: which phone shows the problems with late taps, and which
    line of its sheet is the reason?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. For example the chipset, the RAM, the display (refresh rate), the touch sampling rate, the battery, the OS, the sensors.
2. For example the camera, the weight, the colours.
3. The touch sampling rate (and the refresh rate): taps must reach the game at once.
4. The sensors line: P5 has no gyroscope, which the AR game needs.
5. P5 (4 GB).
6. It hides the problems that most players will meet on weaker phones.
7. The fastest core reaches 3.3 GHz only for a short time, while the SoC is cool.
8. Peak 1000, sustained 800.
9. 4500 ÷ 900 = 5 hours. A video needs much less work than a game.
10. P5: its touch sampling rate is only 120 Hz (and its screen 60 Hz).
:::
